newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia fighting a big blow to tourism centre.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia fighting a big blow to tourism centre.

text.p: Cambodia's main tourist town was virtually deserted of visitors a week after bloody political turmoil broke out in the capital Phnom Penh.

Many restaurants, hotels and travel agencies in Siem Reap, in northwest Cambodia about 25O km (150 miles) from Phnom Penh and the jumping off point for visits to the nearby temples of Angkor, have closed their doors due to the lack of business.

The national airline, Royal Air Cambodge, which suspended flights to Siem Reap due to fighting at Phnom Penh airport last weekend has resumed flights. But airline officials said only one flight a day was being operated instead of the usual seven due to very low demand.
Sun Sitha, a former tour guide who leased a guest house in an attempt to cash in on the tourism boom that followed United Nations-organised elections in 1993, now has 14 empty rooms.
"I've lost $2,000 so far and now I may have to give up," he said.

The handful of tourists who decided to stay in Siem Reap despite the fighting in Phnom Penh and subsequently in the countryside not far from the town found they had the massive Angkor temple complex virtually to themselves.
On Saturday, ticket collectors at the complex's main entrance said they had collected only five receipts that day.
Hotels and guest houses that decided to remain open were all virtually empty on Saturday, and employees in tourism-related businesses have been laid off until customers return.
Many residents said it was not the fighting in Siem Reap province that they feared so much as long-term unemployment.
In the town's market, stalls that usually sell handicrafts and other souvenirs have been locked and deserted for the past week.
Shelling was clearly audible in Siem Reap on Friday, but was much less distinct by Saturday as the fighting had shifted several km (miles) west.

Jacques Lermenier and Murielle Doyien from France, the two foreign tourists to arrive on Saturday's flight from Phnom Penh, said that a visit to Siem Reap was the best alternative to the tension in the capital as they had not been able to get a reservation to Thailand.
"We came to Cambodia to see Angkor Wat and that's what we're going to do," Doyien said.

Lermernier added: "The atmosphere was getting rather heavy in the guest houses in Phnom Penh...some expatriates have been getting rather nervous. That's one of the reasons we wanted to get out of Phnom Penh.

Thousands of foreigners, including tourists, business executives and aid workers, fled Cambodia on emergency evacuation flights after the overthrow of Prince Norodom Ranariddh by the forces of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.
Phnom Penh airport was damaged and closed for several days after the fighting and subsequent looting. Some international flights to neighbouring countries have resumed.
Police in Siem Reap said the Angkor temples were safe to visit and local authorities had not imposed any restrictions apart from closing the road to one remote temple.
